items.title: Sheila Jordan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Well, I think he did that because I was the first singer he ever had.

ctx.x: Is there any way to hang a date or any timeframe for you?

Well, it was before my daughter was born, so it had to be around ‟52 or something. And Duke was off and running again so, you know, I was in the loft by myself. And of course, Duke came back and I got pregnant with my daughter, and the loft… I still had the sessions, though, and Traci would be jumping around. [laughs] Not for long, though. And then I had to move from the loft because when they found out I had a child, the landlord said, you know, “You‟re not supposed to be living here, first of all. But now that…
Oh, that‟s what it is. Belle Isle. Brown, C.: …park for the City of Detroit.

items.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002
items.q: I said, 'Why don't you learn this tune, this minor Blues.' ... 'Mr. P.C.' written by John Coltrane. ... 'Oh what does John Coltrane play?'

ctx.x: The state of jazz these days seems to have found its ways of course into universities and the academic world. Is that a good thing? © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

I knew you were going to ask me this. I’m going to be very honest. In some ways it is and in some ways — and this is only me and I’m not that important as far as my word but I speak but I feel — in some ways it is and in some ways it isn’t. In the ways that it is is it makes people aware of this wonderful music, which is American, which hopefully will close the gap between black and white, I hope. I’d like to see that happen. You play, you play. I don’t know, what color are you? I don’t know, is there a color…
